summary:
Fire in Freefall Data AI Insights is a web dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into clear fire-safety answers. NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository holds 26 combustion investigations with more than 16,000 files. Those results are hard to find, compare and interpret.

Our dashboard loads these records and their experiment tables, including FLEX, ACME, BASS, Saffire and SAME. It lets users rank every investigation for a chosen crew environment: a space station, a lunar habitat, a Mars habitat, a pressurized rover or a custom atmosphere. The scoring rubric is open and its weights can be adjusted. A coverage map shows which oxygen and pressure conditions were tested and which were not. An AI assistant built on Claude answers questions across studies. Every statement cites its NASA source, and code checks each quote and number.

This matters now because Artemis is returning crews to the Moon. Moon Base cabins will hold 30% oxygen or more, which makes materials far more flammable, and no partial-gravity fire data exists yet. The dashboard helps engineers, researchers and students make the next giant leap a safer one.
details:
What it does and how it works
Fire in Freefall Data AI Insights is a web dashboard built on NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. It loads the Combustion Science investigations through the PSI API and turns their experiment tables into structured test runs. These include FLEX, ACME CFI-G, BASS-II and Saffire-I to III. Each test run records fuel, oxygen, pressure, flow and outcome.

Users choose a crew environment: a space station, a lunar habitat or rover, a Mars habitat, or a custom atmosphere. Investigations are then ranked with an open rubric:

  • Atmosphere match: 30 points
  • Fuel and material relevance: 25 points
  • Safety function (prevention, detection or suppression): 20 points
  • Flow match: 15 points
  • Gravity relevance: 10 points

Code computes the measurable parts. Claude judges the other two and must quote evidence from the record. A coverage map shows which oxygen and pressure conditions have and have not been tested. A research assistant answers questions across studies, with a numbered NASA source for every statement.

Benefits

  • Engineers find the studies that apply to their cabin atmosphere in minutes.
  • Researchers export test conditions, with sources, to build and check flammability models.
  • Students learn from real NASA data.
  • Every result links back to its PSI record and DOI.

Intended impact
The goal is safer habitats on the Moon and Mars, where cabins will hold 30% oxygen or more and materials burn more easily. The same research also supports fire safety on Earth: smoke detection, water-mist suppression and firefighter equipment.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL.
  • Back end: Django REST Framework, PostgreSQL.
  • Front end: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, ECharts.
  • AI: Claude models through the Anthropic API.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose and Nginx on one Linux server.
  • Data: NASA PSI open data, licensed CC0.
  • Development: Claude helped write the technical specification and the code.

Creativity
The site’s signature image is a flame that becomes a blue sphere in free fall. The ranking changes with the atmosphere the user picks. The AI can’t invent numbers: every quote and figure it writes is checked automatically against the NASA record. The coverage map makes untested conditions visible, not just the tested ones.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: missing data stays missing, and the site states openly that no partial-gravity data exists.
  • Transparency: the scoring rubric is published and its weights can be changed.
  • Safety: the site is a research aid, not a safety authority.
  • Privacy: there are no accounts and no personal data is collected.
  • Accessibility: dark and light themes, and English only for now.
